analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal government health insurance program covering all Americans' medical and long-term care.
analysis.headline: The bill would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based insurance with a single national health program covering everyone, but it was referred to two House committees in July 1989 and died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a 'USHealth Program' — a government-run health plan covering every U.S. resident regardless of age, disability, or income. It would have covered hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental care, eyeglasses, mental health services, and long-term care, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-provided insurance. It would have been paid for by removing the cap on Medicare payroll taxes, a new tax on wages, a higher cigarette tax, an income surtax if costs ran over, and by ending the tax break for employer health plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain comprehensive health coverage, including the roughly 30 million-plus Americans uninsured at the time and the millions more with coverage that skipped dental care, drugs, eyeglasses, or long-term care. Seniors and disabled people would gain long-term care coverage, low-income families would see premiums and copays waived when they could not afford them, and self-employed people would get a full deduction for health insurance during the transition. Doctors, nurse practitioners, and rural clinics would gain new payment rules and grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All Americans lacking adequate health coverage

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen and permanent resident would be entitled to comprehensive medical and long-term care starting January 1, 1994, without regard to age or disability status [S2][S3].

Covered benefits would include inpatient and psychiatric hospital care, home health, hospice, prescription drugs, dental services and eyeglasses, outpatient mental health, alcohol and drug rehabilitation, and long-term care for chronically ill people [S2].

Out-of-pocket costs would be capped — $600 a year for most services and $1,000 for long-term care — and waived entirely for families whose income fell below the federal poverty level; failure to pay could not cost someone their benefits [S2][S3].
Medicaid would be repealed and replaced, and during the transition Medicaid would be expanded to cover everyone with income below the poverty line by January 1992 [S2].

Providers would be barred from billing patients beyond program payments, and a consumers' bill of rights, ombudsmen, complaint hotlines, and quality-assurance review of hospitals, home health agencies, and HMOs would be created [S2].

analysis.who_pays: High earners would pay the most: the Medicare hospital insurance tax would apply to all wages with no cap, a new excise tax on wages and self-employment income would fund the program, and an income surtax would kick in if program costs exceeded revenues. Employers would lose the tax exclusion for health insurance they provide. Smokers would pay a higher federal cigarette tax. Health insurers, hospitals, and other providers would face global spending caps tied to the size of the economy and centralized payment rates.

drawbacks.text: The financing was heavy on taxes: an uncapped hospital insurance payroll tax, a new excise tax on wages, a higher cigarette tax, an income surtax to cover any shortfall, and repeal of the employer health insurance exclusion, which would have effectively taxed employer health benefits as income [S2][S3].

The bill capped total program spending at 12 percent of gross national product and long-term care spending at 1.1 percent of GNP, and tied all provider payment increases to economic growth — an honest supporter would acknowledge this could force the Board to squeeze payment rates or benefits to stay under the ceilings [S2][S3].

It abolished employer-based and private coverage outright, disrupting insurance arrangements tens of millions of people had, and left the Board with broad discretion to set payment rates and adjust coverage categories [S2].
It steered enrollment toward HMOs by raising their payment to 100 percent of cost and directing a national campaign to encourage people to join them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the upside was enormous — universal coverage including services almost no American insurance covered at the time, with cost-sharing capped and waived for the poor — and the cost was a large, broadly shared tax increase concentrated on high earners, employers, and smokers, plus hard spending caps that could constrain payments to providers. The design was ambitious but not reckless; the main risk was whether the fixed budget could absorb long-term care, the fastest-growing cost. The bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then split among three subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Roybal of California introduced the bill on July 24, 1989, joined by Reps. Rangel, Dymally, and Ackerman, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees [S3][S5].

Within two weeks it was divided among three subcommittees — Ways and Means' Social Security subcommittee, Energy and Commerce's Health subcommittee, and the Health and the Environment subcommittee — the last action of any kind in the bill's history [S5].
It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and no further action is recorded before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].
It ended the Congress with 11 cosponsors, all House Democrats, out of 435 members [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health coverage status quo — private insurers and employers whose insurance arrangements the bill would have abolished, and providers facing global budget caps — was left untouched, because the bill died quietly in committee without a debate or vote. The uninsured and underinsured gained nothing, and the existing system's costs continued to grow through the 1990s.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the coverage status quo

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health programs

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is known only from sponsorship: all 12 supporters were Democrats, no Republicans cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committees that held the bill took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have abolished the private coverage market — repealing Medicaid, replacing employer-based insurance, and making the public program the primary payer — but it directed the new Board to use insurance companies as claims processors (carriers) wherever practicable, locking insurers into an administrative role. Their core business of selling coverage would have disappeared; their processing contracts would have survived.

The bill raised the federal payment rate for HMO enrollees from 95 percent to 100 percent of cost and required a national campaign encouraging people to enroll with HMOs, while requiring HMOs to cover all program services and submit to quality review.

All provider payment increases would have been tied to growth in per-capita GNP, with total spending capped at 12 percent of the economy — a global budget that would have limited hospital, physician, and long-term care revenues. Rural facilities and clinics, however, would have gained new grants and payment rules.

The bill repealed the tax exclusion for employer health insurance contributions, meaning employers could no longer deliver tax-free health benefits, and they would have paid uncapped payroll taxes. Workers would have gotten public coverage in exchange.
The bill increased the federal excise tax on cigarettes to help fund the program, a cost passed to smokers and borne by the industry in lower sales.

The Medicare hospital insurance tax would have applied to all wages with no dollar cap after 1989, and an income surtax would have covered any gap between program costs and revenues — the largest tax burden falling on the highest earners.
